questions.text: A Dao timber beam is specified for a structure with occasional water splash. What limitation applies?

options.text: Dao resists decay but not termites; it is unsuitable for splash zones without treatment.
Dao has no resistance classification and must be treated for any durability, especially in environments with high humidity.
Dao is adequate because it resists decay; splash water does not attract termites, making it a viable option for such conditions.
Dao sapwood must be completely removed before use to prevent any potential decay or insect infestation.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Incorrect: Dao IS in the classification table with decay resistance.
rationale.d: Incorrect logic. Even if decay resistance exists, termite risk is real in Philippine regions.
rationale.correct: Dao is decay-resistant only. Splash zones carry both fungal decay risk AND termite risk in tropical climates. Dao lacks termite protection.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NatCor durability classification; Philippine Forestry Code Section 111

questions.text: A timber specification states: 'Narra heartwood, maximum 3% sapwood per edge.' Is this specification _more restrictive_ or _less restrictive_ than NatCor standards?

options.text: More restrictive. NatCor allows up to 5%; this spec reduces the limit to 3%.
Less restrictive. NatCor allows only heartwood; this spec permits any sapwood.
Equivalent. NatCor uses a 3–5% range with no fixed maximum.
Not comparable. Sapwood limits apply only to treated timber, not heartwood.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: NatCor explicitly permits up to 5%; it does not prohibit sapwood.
rationale.d: NatCor does not specify a variable range; 5% is the threshold.
rationale.correct: NatCor permits 5% sapwood (on linear dimension) as the maximum when heartwood ≥90% per face. A 3% limit is stricter, reducing acceptable sapwood to improve durability margin.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NatCor Section 3.2; specification engineering best practices

questions.text: A structural designer substitutes Yakal for a specified Narra timber in a ground-contact foundation beam. What compliance issue arises?

options.text: Yakal has documented decay resistance but lacks dual (decay+termite) classification equivalent to Narra for ground-contact without treatment.
Yakal is listed as a decay-resistant alternative and is acceptable as a direct substitution, provided it meets all other structural requirements.
Yakal resists termites better than Narra but is weaker in bending; the design must be strengthened to compensate for this.
The substitution is valid as long as the same allowable stress values are maintained, which may require additional verification.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Yakal does not appear in the NatCor durability schedule at any resistance level.
rationale.d: Strength properties and durability are independent. Maintaining stress values does not satisfy durability requirements.
rationale.correct: Yakal is NOT in the NatCor durability classification table. It may have strength, but durability claims without explicit standard approval are non-compliant. Ground-contact use requires explicit classification.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NatCor Section 3.2; Philippine Building Code compliance requirements

questions.text: Identify the resistance profile of Tangile timber in structural use.

options.text: Decay resistant, termite susceptible
Termite resistant, decay susceptible
Both decay and termite resistant
Neither decay nor termite resistant; treatment always required

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Tangile is classified as decay-resistant only. It shares the profile of Dao: good fungal durability, zero termite protection.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A design team discovers that specified Narra is in short supply and proposes chemically treating Dao timber instead. Evaluate this substitution strategy.

options.text: Valid. Treated Dao will provide both decay and termite resistance equivalent to untreated Narra when properly applied.
Invalid. NatCor prohibits substitution of treated timber; only naturally durable species are permitted for ground-contact use, ensuring long-term performance.
Valid for decay, but termite protection depends on treatment type and application depth; verify treatment compliance with Philippine Building Code.
Partially valid. Treatment adds decay resistance but cannot guarantee the long-term termite immunity of naturally durable species, which is critical for structural integrity.

rationale.a: Treatment is effective, but 'equivalent' requires specific verification of treatment type, retention levels (kg/m³), and penetration depth—not automatic.
rationale.b: NatCor does not prohibit treated timber; it recognizes treatment as a valid durability strategy when natural durability is insufficient.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Chemical treatment can add both decay and termite protection to Dao, making it functionally equivalent to untreated Narra IF the treatment specification (e.g., copper-based, boron salts, oil-borne preservatives) is appropriate for the hazard class and application depth is verified per PD1096 Rule VIII Section 809 (Wood) or FPRDI treatment standards or equivalent.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: Philippine Building Code Section 2401; NatCor Section 3.3 (treated timber provisions); ASEAN TCS 4-2019

questions.text: A Kamagong beam is placed in a brackish estuary environment subject to saltwater splash and submerged daily cycles. What design approach is necessary?

options.text: Kamagong's natural dual resistance (decay + termites) is sufficient for this marine exposure; no additional treatment is required.
Even Kamagong's heartwood will gradually degrade under saltwater exposure; protective coating or concrete encasement should be specified.
Kamagong is unsuitable for saltwater; only treated softwood is acceptable, especially in environments with high salinity and tidal fluctuations.
Kamagong resists organic decay but not salt crystallization damage; structural monitoring intervals should be specified, particularly during seasonal changes.

rationale.a: Terrestrial durability ≠ marine durability. Saltwater environments exceed the scope of NatCor resistance classification.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: Kamagong IS durable in terrestrial harsh environments; marine exposure is a separate class of hazard.
rationale.correct: NatCor classification covers terrestrial decay (fungi) and termites only, not salt-water-induced crystallization, corrosion-cell mechanisms, or extended submersion. Kamagong heartwood will eventually deteriorate under continuous saltwater exposure despite high natural durability.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NatCor Section 3.2 (terrestrial classification scope); ASEAN TCS 4-2019; ISO 12944 marine durability standards

questions.text: Which Philippine timber species provide BOTH decay and termite resistance without chemical treatment?

options.text: Narra and Kamagong
Narra and Dao
Tangile and Kamagong
Yakal and Molave

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Dao has decay resistance only; it offers NO termite protection.
rationale.d: Kamagong is correct, but Tangile has decay resistance only.
rationale.correct: Narra, Kamagong, and Molave have documented natural resistance to both decay and termites per FPRDI and forestry standards. This is the foundational durability pair in Philippine timber standards.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: FPRDI Timber Durability Classification or Philippine Wood Handbook

questions.text: Explain why heartwood is essential for decay and termite resistance, while sapwood is not.

options.text: Heartwood contains extractive compounds that inhibit fungal and insect colonization; sapwood is nutrient-rich and vulnerable to both.
Heartwood is older and therefore harder; sapwood is newer and softer, making it more susceptible to environmental damage and pest infestation
Heartwood is chemically treated in the tree; sapwood is left untreated and lacks the natural protective compounds found in heartwood
Sapwood naturally repels moisture; heartwood absorbs it and must be treated, which is a misconception as heartwood is naturally more resistant

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Hardness is unrelated to resistance; mechanical strength and durability are distinct properties.
rationale.d: Trees do not chemically treat their own sapwood; the distinction is biological extractive accumulation.
rationale.correct: Extractives (natural antimicrobial compounds such as tannins and terpenoids) concentrate in the heartwood as the tree ages. Sapwood lacks these and is nutritionally attractive to decomposers and insects.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A foundation beam specification requires 'durable timber suitable for continuous soil contact in high-termite-pressure regions.' Which of the following satisfies this requirement without additional treatment?

options.text: Narra heartwood or Kamagong heartwood, with sapwood ≤5% per edge and ≥90% heartwood per face.
Dao or Tangile heartwood, with full sapwood removal and protective membrane applied to all surfaces for enhanced durability.
Any Philippine hardwood listed in the timber grades table, provided allowable stresses are verified and documented in compliance reports.
Treated Yakal with third-party durability certification, ensuring compliance with local building codes and standards.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: Dao and Tangile lack termite resistance; even with full sapwood removal, they remain susceptible.
rationale.d: Grading tables address strength, not durability. A species in the grades table may have no durability classification.
rationale.correct: Only Narra and Kamagong provide natural dual resistance (decay + termites) with the sapwood acceptance rule built into the standard. This satisfies the requirement without additional measures.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A Narra timber piece shows sapwood on one edge representing 7% of the piece length, with heartwood comprising 93% of each face. Is this acceptable for ground-contact structural use?

options.text: Yes. Sapwood is within the 5% tolerance and each face shows ≥90% heartwood.
No. Any visible sapwood disqualifies the piece for ground-contact use.
Yes, but only if the sapwood is sealed with a protective coating.
No. The 7% sapwood exceeds the allowable 5% threshold.

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: NatCor permits sapwood only if it is ≤5% on linear dimension. Here, 7% sapwood exceeds the 5% threshold. Despite 93% heartwood per face meeting the 90% rule, the 7% sapwood on the edge disqualifies the piece for ground-contact use.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.
